title: Result and Option Together
story: Your config system has two layers: a key might not exist at all (Option), AND even if it exists, its value might be invalid (Result). You need both types working together — a `Result[Option[Int], Str]` that says 'the lookup worked, but there's either a value or nothing there.'
why: Combining Result and Option models real-world scenarios where operations can fail AND values can be absent — nested types express complex states precisely.
analogy: Result[Option[T], E] is like calling a library — the call itself might fail (Result) if your phone dies, and the book might be checked out (Option) even if the call went through.
try_it: Add more config keys: "volume" -> "75", "brightness" -> "abc" (invalid), "contrast" -> None. Write a `get_all_settings` function that parses all 5 keys and prints a summary: how many succeeded, how many failed, and how many were missing.
tips: `Result[Option[T], E]` has THREE states: Ok(Some(val)), Ok(None), Err(e) — handle all three
Use `?` on the outer Result, then match on the inner Option
Name functions that return both types clearly: `find_and_validate`, `lookup_or_error`
common_mistakes: Forgetting the third state — `Ok(None)` is different from `Err(...)`. One means 'exists but empty,' the other means 'doesn't exist'
Nesting too deep — `Result[Option[Result[...]]]` is a sign you should simplify your design
Using `unwrap_or` on a `Result[Option[T], E]` — you need two levels of unwrapping: first the Result, then the Option
